summary.text: Time is the continuous progression of existence from past through present to future, used to sequence events and compare how long they last.
Physics defines it operationally as what a clock reads, a count of repeating events such as the SI second, and treats it as part of spacetime.
Time can be dilated by speed or gravity, and reconciling its role in relativity and quantum mechanics is an open problem.

facts.label: SI unit
facts.value: The second, defined using caesium atoms

facts.label: Early clocks
facts.value: Periodic motion like the sun, moon and pendulums

facts.label: Two tools
facts.value: Calendars for long periods, clocks for short ones

facts.label: Julius Caesar
facts.value: His 45 BC reforms gave Rome a solar calendar

facts.label: Spacetime
facts.value: Events get three space coordinates and one time

items.prompt: A friend asks you to define time without using words like 'duration' or 'later'. How does physics get around this circularity?

options.label: It defines time as what a clock reads
It defines time as the fourth space direction
It declares time to be undefinable
It defines time by the length of a day

items.explain: To avoid a circular definition, physics operationally defines time as what a clock reads, a count of repeating events such as the SI second.

items.prompt: Two observers in very different situations disagree about whether two events were simultaneous. What does physics make of this?

options.label: One observer must have a broken clock
The idea of 'now' is relative between observers
Light travels at different speeds for each
Simultaneity only fails in quantum systems

items.explain: Event coordinates can vary for different observers, making ideas like now and here relative.

items.prompt: A calendar based only on twelve moon cycles slowly slides out of step with the seasons. What fix did lunisolar calendars use?

options.label: Shortening each month
Skipping the moon entirely
Adding a thirteenth month in some years
Making every year have 354 days

items.explain: Twelve lunar months fall short of a full year, so lunisolar calendars add a thirteenth month to some years.

items.prompt: An astronaut travelling at extreme speed returns and has aged a little less than her twin. Which idea fits?

options.label: Time can pass slower depending on velocity
Clocks always run at one fixed rate
Her clock was synchronised badly
Time ran backwards for a while

items.explain: Time can be dilated by velocity and matter, noticeable only in extreme conditions such as relativistic speeds.

items.prompt: You need to mark a moment three weeks from now at 4 p.m. Which pair of tools does this take?

options.label: Two calendars
A calendar for the day and a clock for the hour
Two clocks
A clock for the day and a calendar for the hour

items.explain: A calendar organises periods longer than a day and a clock handles periods shorter than a day; together they mark a moment from a reference point.

items.prompt: Why do physicists say they still lack a full account of time at the smallest scales?

options.label: Clocks are too inaccurate to test it
Relativity and quantum mechanics treat time differently
Light travels at different speeds there
Time stops existing below the second

items.explain: Quantum mechanics treats time as a universal absolute parameter while general relativity uses independent clocks, and no accepted theory reconciles them.

paragraphs.heading: What time is
paragraphs.text: Time is the ongoing flow of existence from the past, through the present, into the future, in an order that seems impossible to reverse. We use it to put events in order, to compare how long they last and the gaps between them, and to measure how fast things change. It is often called the fourth dimension, alongside the three dimensions of space. Even so, a definition that works in every field without going in circles has always escaped scholars.

paragraphs.heading: What a clock reads
paragraphs.text: In physics, time is a basic idea needed to define other quantities, such as velocity. To avoid a circular definition, physics defines it by how it is measured: time is what a clock reads, meaning a count of events that repeat, such as the SI second. This helps with practical measurement, but it says nothing about what time really is.

paragraphs.heading: Time and space together
paragraphs.text: Physicists give every event four coordinates, three for space and one for time, in what they call the spacetime continuum. Different observers may give the same rocket launch or supernova different coordinates, so ideas like now and here are relative. Light takes the same time to cross a given distance for every observer, so all observers agree on time as a link between cause and effect. Time can also be stretched by speed and by matter, though the effect only matters near light speed or in the pull of black holes.

paragraphs.heading: An open problem
paragraphs.text: Quantum mechanics treats time as one universal, absolute parameter, unlike general relativity, where clocks run independently. Fitting these two views together is called the problem of time. As of 2026, no theory of quantum general relativity has been generally accepted.

paragraphs.heading: Clocks and calendars
paragraphs.text: Measuring time, or chronometry, takes two main forms. A calendar is a mathematical tool for organising stretches longer than a day, and a clock is a physical device for stretches shorter than a day. Together they mark a moment counted from a starting point called an epoch. Time is one of the seven fundamental quantities in the SI system, and its base unit, the second, is defined by the frequency of an electronic transition in caesium atoms. Older ways of keeping time watched regular motions, such as the sun crossing the sky, the phases of the moon and a swinging pendulum.

paragraphs.heading: The first calendars
paragraphs.text: Objects from the Paleolithic suggest people were using the moon to count time at least 6,000 years ago. Lunar calendars were among the first, with years made of 12 or 13 lunar months, which is 354 or 384 days. A calendar of only twelve lunar months lets the seasons drift unless extra days or months are slipped in. Lunisolar calendars fix this by adding a thirteenth month to some years, covering the gap to a full year of about 365.24 days. Later, the reforms of Julius Caesar in 45 BC moved the Roman world onto a solar calendar.
